title: The First Flock
subtitle: The Church's Calling to Care for Pastors and Their Families
blurb: The man you call to feed you is starving, and you have not noticed. This is a book about the reciprocal duty a congregation owes the shepherd it ordained to shepherd it — and about the first flock no one counts, the family inside the parsonage who absorb the cost of a ministry they never chose. It is written to the church as much as to the pastor, because the pastor cannot fix this, and the church has been pretending it is not the one holding the knife.

chapters.title: The Man You Are Consuming
chapters.summary: The congregation has learned to treat the pastor as a resource to be drawn down rather than a person to be carried. This chapter names the consumption and refuses to let it hide behind affection.
chapters.body:
There is a man in your church who knows the names of your dead. He buried your father. He sat in the hospital corridor while you decided whether to remove the ventilator. He prayed over the marriage you were too proud to admit was failing, and he kept the secret. He has a key to the building and a key to your worst night, and you have decided, without ever deciding it, that this is simply what he is for.

Not a person. A function.

I have been that man, and I have watched congregations do to other men what was done to me, and the cruelty of it is that it never feels like cruelty. It feels like need. The church does not gather on Sunday intending to bleed its pastor dry. It gathers hungry, and the pastor is the one standing at the front holding bread, and over years the hunger learns the shape of his hands and stops seeing his face. Richard Baxter, three and a half centuries ago, wrote a book to pastors called *The Reformed Pastor* in which he begged ministers to take heed first to themselves before they took heed to the flock. We read it as a charge to the pastor. We have never once read it as a charge to the people who are wearing him down to the bone.

The word I want is *consumption*, and I choose it knowing it once named a disease. Tuberculosis was called consumption because the body was eaten from within while the face still smiled. That is the precise condition of the American pastorate. From the outside, vigor. The sermon lands. The lights are on. The man shakes four hundred hands and remembers a hundred names. Inside, something is being eaten, and the smiling is part of the symptom.

The research on this is not subtle, even when we keep it general. Across denominations and across the years, studies of clergy report the same pattern: high rates of exhaustion, isolation, depression, and a quiet stream of men leaving the ministry not because their theology changed but because their bodies and marriages gave out. I will not pretend to a precise figure, because the precise figures get weaponized and forgotten. The shape is enough. The shape is a man who entered ministry on fire and left it as ash, and a congregation that never understood it was the fire.

Hear what I am not saying. I am not saying the pastor is a victim and the people are villains. That story is too clean, and I distrust clean stories about sin because I have never lived inside one. I am saying something harder. I am saying that consumption is a relationship, and both parties are inside it. The pastor who will not say no is feeding the thing that eats him. The man who answers the phone at midnight every night for a decade and calls it faithfulness has confused his own martyrdom with the gospel, and there is a kind of pride that wears itself out on purpose so it never has to admit it is pride. I know that man. I have been that man at three in the morning, congratulating myself on the very exhaustion that was a sin against my wife.

So the indictment runs in both directions. But this book is written to the church first, because the church is the body with the power, and the pastor is the one with his back against the wall, and it is dishonest to spend a book lecturing the cornered man about his posture.

Consider what you ask of him without asking. You expect him available, which means you expect him never fully present anywhere — not at his son's game, not at his own table, not in his own grief — because availability is a promise to be interrupted, and a man who is always interruptible is never anywhere. You expect him competent across a span of professions no one human holds: scholar, orator, counselor, administrator, fundraiser, comforter, prophet, plumber when the baptistry leaks. You expect him to model a peace he is not given time to possess. And then, the cruelest expectation of all, you expect him to need nothing, because his needing would frighten you. A pastor who admits he is afraid, lonely, or doubting threatens the arrangement by which you outsourced your own faith to his apparent certainty.

Paul knew this arrangement and refused to flatter it. Writing to a church that adored its visiting celebrities and tolerated its founder, he said the strangest thing: *I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?* (2 Corinthians 12:15). Spend and be spent. He used the language of currency on purpose, and he asked the unbearable question underneath it — does loving you cost me your love? The answer, often, is yes. The pastor who tells a church the truth it does not want gets spent twice: once in the telling and once in the punishment for having told.

There is a moment in the life of nearly every long-tenured pastor when he realizes that the people who depend on him most are the people who know him least. They know his voice. They do not know his sabbath, his marriage, his fear, the toll of carrying their secrets in a body that also has to carry his own. Eugene Peterson spent decades warning that we had turned pastors into shopkeepers running a religious store, anxious about the numbers, performing a relevance that has nothing to do with the cure of souls. The shopkeeper is consumed by his customers and calls it service. He cannot afford to be a person. The store would close.

I want to say the verdict plainly and let it sit, because the rest of this book is the working-out of it. You are not loving your pastor. You are spending him. And the difference between love and spending is that love asks what the other person costs and is willing to pay it, while spending asks what the other person can produce and draws it down until the account is empty.

The first flock is not the congregation. We will come to that — to the wife who married a man and got a movement, to the children who never volunteered to be public. But before we get there, the church has to confront the smaller, plainer fact at the front of the room every Sunday. The man feeding you is hungry. He has learned not to say so, because the last time a pastor said so within your hearing, you found another church or found a way to call him weak.

I am asking you to look at his face. Not the face he wears at the door, the practiced warmth he can summon on no sleep. The other face, the one in the car before he walks in. You have never seen it. He has made sure of that. And the making-sure is the wound.

There is a duty here, and the body of this book is its anatomy. The shepherd is also a sheep. The man who carries you needs carrying. And a church that cannot care for the one it ordained to care for it has misunderstood the gospel it claims, because the gospel was never a transaction in which the strong feed the weak from an inexhaustible supply. It was a body, knit together, where the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you (1 Corinthians 12:21). Your pastor is a part of that body. He bleeds when you cut him. You have not been watching the blood.

Start watching.
chapters.verdict: You are not loving your pastor. You are spending him.
reflect: When did you last ask your pastor a question with no agenda attached to the answer?
What would change in your church if the pastor were treated as a sheep and not only a shepherd?
Whose burnout have you mistaken for laziness, or whose silence have you mistaken for peace?

chapters.title: The First Flock
chapters.summary: Scripture names the pastor's household before it names the congregation, yet the church has reversed the order and called the reversal devotion. This chapter establishes the family as the shepherd's first and primary charge.
chapters.body:
Paul is listing the qualifications for an overseer, and the list is what you would expect — above reproach, sober, not violent, not greedy — until he says a thing the modern church reads past as though it were filler. *He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?* (1 Timothy 3:4–5).

Read the logic, because it is exact. The household is not a credential the pastor clears on the way to the real work. The household is the test case of the real work. The family is the proof that the man can shepherd at all. Paul is saying that the church is the second flock. The first flock lives in his house.

We have inverted this so thoroughly that to state it plainly sounds like heresy to the very congregations that confess the verse. We have built a ministry culture in which the man who neglects his family for the church is celebrated as devoted, and the man who guards his family from the church is suspected of being uncommitted. We have made the sin look like sanctity. And we did not do it by accident. We did it because a pastor who pours himself out on the congregation is more useful to the congregation than a pastor who reserves himself for his wife and sons. The inversion serves us. That is why it survives.

I have five sons. I will not narrate their private lives in a book, because they did not ask to be born into a man's vocation, and the first thing a pastor's family is owed is the right not to be material. But I will say the general thing, the thing every pastor's family knows. There is a competition for the father, and the church does not believe it is competing, and that disbelief is what makes it win. A man having an affair knows he is betraying his wife. A man giving every night to the church tells himself he is serving God, and the self-deception is total, and the wife at home with the cold dinner cannot fight it because she would have to argue against God.

This is the particular cruelty of ministry. In most professions, the family can at least name the rival. The man married to his career has a career to resent. The pastor's family is asked to resent the kingdom of God, and they will not do it, so they swallow the resentment and it becomes something worse — a low, theological loneliness, a sense that they come second to Jesus and must never say so, because saying so feels like apostasy. Children raised in that house learn early that the faith took their father. Some of them never forgive it. Some of them never forgive God for it, and we call them prodigals and shake our heads, and we never ask whether the church helped raise them to run.

Hear the verse again. *If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?* Paul is not making the family a stepping stone. He is making it a sacrament of sorts — a visible sign that the invisible competence is real. The man who shepherds his wife with tenderness and his children with patient, present love has shown the church what kind of shepherd he is. The man who is magnificent on Sunday and absent on Tuesday has shown the church the same thing, and the church has chosen not to see it because Sunday is what the church wanted.

There is a hard word here for pastors, and I will say it to myself first. Brother, the inversion is not only done to you. You collude with it. The church may pull, but you say yes, and your yes is often not love but a hunger for the affirmation the church gives and the home cannot. The home does not applaud. The home sees you with your collar off and your defenses down, and the home asks you to be ordinary, and ordinary is the one thing the applauded man cannot bear to be. So you go where they clap. You call it ministry. Your wife calls it Tuesday, and Wednesday, and the anniversary you moved for the elder meeting.

Jesus asked the question that should end every pastor's self-justification. *What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?* (Mark 8:36). Make it parochial. What does it profit a man to gain the whole congregation and forfeit his sons? You will not be asked at the judgment how the church grew. You will be asked whether you loved the people God actually gave you, and the first ones he gave you are asleep down the hall while you write the sermon about loving people.

But this is a book to the church, and the church has its own repentance. You must stop rewarding the inversion. When your pastor guards an evening, do not let your face fall. When he takes his anniversary, do not call him the day before with the thing that could have waited. When he says my son has a game, do not say of course, go, and then remember it at his review as a softness. You are training him, every day, in what you will applaud and what you will punish, and right now you are applauding the slow destruction of his home and calling it his heart for the church.

Brueggemann taught a generation to read the prophets as men who refused the dominant arrangement, who would not let the empire's version of normal pass as the will of God. There is an empire in the church, and its normal is a pastor consumed, and the prophetic act — the act of resistance — is a congregation that says to its shepherd: go home. We will survive a night without you. We would rather have a whole man for thirty years than a broken hero for ten.

A man who loses his family to save your church has saved nothing. He has built a house on the lot where his own house used to stand, and one day the new house will praise him in a building program, and the old house, the first flock, will be empty, and the wind will move through it. You will not hear that wind on Sunday. He hears it every night.

The order is set by God, not by preference. First the household, then the church. A congregation that loves its pastor will defend that order even against the pastor's own willingness to betray it. That is what care looks like when it grows up. Not taking more of him. Helping him keep the part of him that was never yours to take.
chapters.verdict: A man who loses his family to save your church has saved nothing.
reflect: Does your church's schedule assume the pastor has a family, or assume he does not?
When the pastor protects an evening at home, do you read it as faithfulness or as failure?
What have you asked of your pastor that you would never ask of yourself in your own marriage?

chapters.title: The Loneliness at the Center
chapters.summary: The pastor is surrounded by people and known by almost none of them, and the structure of the role manufactures the isolation. This chapter examines the particular solitude of standing at the front.
chapters.body:
A pastor can be the most surrounded man in town and the most alone. Both at once. The crowd is not company. The crowd is the very thing that produces the solitude, the way a stage produces the dark beyond the lights — the more brightly you are lit, the less you can see who is out there, and the less they can see of you that is not performance.

I want to describe the loneliness precisely, because it is not the ordinary loneliness of a man with no friends. It is the loneliness of a man with four hundred relationships and no peers. Everyone in the building has a relationship with him. None of them is mutual in the way friendship requires. They come to him with their burdens and he carries them, and the carrying is one-directional by design, and a man who only ever carries and is never carried becomes, over years, a kind of beast of burden who has forgotten he was meant to be a brother.

Here is the structural trap, and I want the church to understand it as structure and not as the pastor's personality flaw. He cannot confide in the congregation, because his struggles become their crisis. Tell the deacon you are exhausted and questioning your call, and by Wednesday it is a leadership concern. Tell the small group your marriage is strained, and you have handed them a thing they do not know how to hold, and some of them will hold it badly, and you will spend a year managing the fallout of your own honesty. So the pastor learns to perform fineness. He gets very good at it. The performance is not vanity. It is survival inside a structure that punishes his transparency.

And he cannot easily confide outside the congregation either, because pastors are kept too busy and too poor and too geographically scattered to maintain real friendships with other pastors, and there is a quiet competition between churches that poisons the well before he can drink from it. Will the pastor across town keep his confidence, or file it away? Is that man a friend or a rival for the same shrinking pool of attenders? The structure isolates horizontally as well as vertically. Above him, the people he serves. Beside him, the men who could understand him but are kept at arm's length by busyness and suspicion. Below him — no one. There is no below. He is at the bottom of the care he is supposed to provide and there is no floor.

I built the Pastors Connection Network because I could not breathe. I will not dress it up as strategy. I was a pastor with no pastor, and I went looking for the brotherhood that the structure had stolen, and I found that nearly every man I called was as starved as I was, and most of them had assumed the starvation was unique to them and therefore shameful. That is the genius of the isolation. It convinces each man that he alone is failing, that the other pastors have the peace he lacks, and so he hides the very wound that, named aloud, would have connected him to every other man in the room. We were a congregation of the lonely, each certain he was the only one.

Scripture does not romanticize the solitary leader. It pities him. Moses, the most capable man in Israel, was being destroyed by carrying the people alone, and his father-in-law looked at him and said the plain thing the surrounding crowd could not see: *What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone* (Exodus 18:17–18). Not able. The verdict was not that Moses was weak. The verdict was that the arrangement was impossible and would grind even a great man to powder. The solution was not more grit. It was shared load. It was other men.

Even Jesus, who could have done everything alone, did not. He chose twelve, and within the twelve he chose three, and on the night he was most afraid he took the three to the garden and asked them to stay awake with him (Matthew 26:38). He did not need their competence. He needed their presence. He needed not to be alone in the dark, and he was the Son of God. If the Son of God wanted company in his agony, what arrogance has convinced your pastor that he should be able to bear his alone — and what cruelty in the church has agreed with that arrogance and left him to it?

The church has a role here, and it is not the role of fixing him. You cannot be his peer; the structure forbids it, and the people who try usually want something from the access. But you can do two things. You can make it safe for him to be a human being who is sometimes wrong, sometimes tired, sometimes afraid, by not punishing the first sign of it. And you can release him to the friendships he needs — protect his time with other pastors, pay for the retreat, cover the pulpit so he can go away and be a man among men who understand. Do not begrudge him the days he spends with people who are not you. Those days are what keep him alive for you.

There is a particular sin I have watched congregations commit, and it is the sin of consuming the pastor's vulnerability when he finally offers it. He opens, at last, a small door. He admits a struggle. And instead of treating the moment as sacred, the church treats it as information — assesses it, discusses it, decides whether it disqualifies him. He learns the lesson instantly and forever. The door closes and does not open again. You had one chance to receive his honesty as a brother and you received it as a board, and now he will perform fineness until the day he resigns or collapses, and you will say you never saw it coming.

A shepherd with no shepherd is a sheep dying in the open. That is the verdict, and I mean the image. A sheep separated from the flock, with no one watching, is the easiest thing in the world for the wolf to take. We picture the pastor as the one with the rod and staff. We never picture him as the lone animal on the hillside at dusk, no fold, no flock, no one counting whether he came home. But that is what we have made of him. The man who counts everyone is counted by no one.

The loneliness will not be solved by a program. It will be solved by people who decide that this particular man, who has carried so many, will himself be carried — not because he is the pastor, but because he is a brother, and brothers do not let each other die alone in the open. The question is whether your church contains such people, or only such crowds.
chapters.verdict: A shepherd with no shepherd is a sheep dying in the open.
reflect: Who in your church knows the pastor without needing anything from him?
Have you ever made it safe for your pastor to be wrong in front of you?
When was the last time you offered your pastor friendship instead of feedback?

chapters.title: The Woman Who Married a Man and Got a Movement
chapters.summary: The pastor's wife inherited a role she never chose, with expectations no one wrote down and everyone enforces. This chapter defends her right to be a person and not an unpaid extension of the church's staff.
chapters.body:
She married a man. She stood at the front of a church or a courthouse and made promises to a person — to his laugh, his stubbornness, the way he is in the morning. She did not stand there and vow to run the women's ministry. She did not promise to play piano, host the small group, smile through the potluck, and absorb the congregation's opinions about her clothes, her children, and the warmth of her welcome at the door. Nobody handed her that contract to read. The church wrote it after the wedding, in invisible ink, and has been enforcing it ever since.

The pastor's wife is the most quietly used person in the American church. I say used and I mean it. She receives a job description she never accepted, a salary of zero, a public role with no authority to refuse it, and a level of scrutiny that would be called harassment in any other setting. Her marriage is a fishbowl. Her parenting is a sermon illustration whether she consents or not. Her bad day is a topic. And if she withdraws to protect herself, the congregation reads the withdrawal as coldness and adds it to the list of disappointments it keeps about her, the list she is not allowed to see and can never answer.

I will not tell my wife's story; it is hers, and the first dignity I can offer the women in this position is to refuse to make them into illustrations even while defending them. But I have sat with enough pastors' wives, through the network and across years, to know the pattern, and the pattern is grief wearing a smile. These are women who often love the church and love their husbands and feel, underneath, that they have been slowly erased — that they exist now as a function of someone else's calling, that the congregation does not actually know them and has never tried, that they are recognized everywhere and known nowhere. Recognized and unknown. It is the loneliness of the last chapter, but worse, because at least the pastor chose the vocation. She married into a life she is asked to live as if she had been ordained to it, and she was not.

The expectations are rarely spoken, which is what makes them inescapable. If they were written down, she could negotiate. Because they float in the air as assumption, she can only fail them. She is expected to be present at everything but never to overshadow. To be warm but not familiar. To be involved but not controlling. To dress well but not too well. To raise visibly excellent children on a salary that cannot fund excellence and a husband who is gone. To never complain, because complaint from the parsonage is treated as ingratitude toward the God who called them. She is the one woman in the church who is not allowed to have a hard week, because her hard week threatens the institution's belief that the first family has it all together.

Scripture honors women in ministry without consuming them. Paul names Priscilla as a fellow worker, not as Aquila's accessory, and notably names her first in several mentions — a woman with her own standing, her own teaching, her own gift (Romans 16:3). Phoebe carried the letter to the Romans and is called a servant of the church and a patron of many (Romans 16:1–2). These women ministered. They were not drafted into ministry as the unpaid appendage of a man's job. There is a chasm between a woman who chooses to serve out of her own gifting and calling, and a woman who is conscripted into service because she happens to be married to the preacher. The first is a sister with a vocation. The second is a hostage with a casserole.

Hear the distinction, church, because it is the whole point. Offering the pastor's wife ministry is honor. Assigning it to her is exploitation. The difference is consent, and consent requires that she be free to say no without it costing her standing, her reputation, or her husband's job. Right now, in most churches, she is not free to say no. Her no would be discussed. Her no would be a problem. And a service that cannot be declined is not service. It is servitude with worship music.

There is a wound that comes from this, and it has a particular flavor. The pastor's wife often loses her own faith community precisely because she is married to its leader. Where does she go to be cared for? She cannot be a normal member of her own church — every relationship is shaped by who her husband is. She cannot fall apart in the women's group; she is the women's group's quiet supervisor. She has no pastor either, because her pastor is her husband, and her husband is the one whose ministry is the source of the very pressure she needs pastoring through. She is inside the institution and exiled from its comforts at the same time. The fish in the fishbowl is never offered a drink of water.

I want to speak to the church and then to the pastor. Church: find out who she actually is. Not what she does. Who she is. What she loved before she was the pastor's wife. What gift God put in her that has nothing to do with your expectations. Make room for her to be a person in your midst, free to serve where she is called and free to rest where she is not, and protect her from the gossip that treats her as public property. She is not staff. She did not sign on. Treat her as you would want a stranger to treat your own wife after watching her for a decade through a window.

And pastor — this last word is the hardest and it is mine to carry too. She is your first congregant, and you are likely her worst-served member. You shepherd hundreds and bring home to her the exhausted remnant, the man with nothing left, and you ask her to be fed by the leftovers of a feast you served to people who will leave the church the moment a better band comes to town. You have a wife who is starving in the kitchen of the restaurant where you cook for everyone else. Feed her first. Paul said a man should love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). For her. Not for the congregation that bears the name of the church. For the woman. The actual woman.

She vowed to love a man, not to serve your committee. The committee will not say so at her funeral, but it will have spent her all the same, and the man she married will stand at the graveside knowing he let it happen, and the church will bring a very nice meal afterward. Do better now, while she is alive and the smile still has a person behind it.
chapters.verdict: She vowed to love a man, not to serve your committee.
reflect: What does your church silently expect of the pastor's wife that it expects of no other woman in the congregation?
Has anyone offered her ministry, or only assigned it?
Do you know her well enough to know what she actually loves, or only well enough to know what she does?

chapters.title: The Children Who Never Volunteered
chapters.summary: Pastors' kids carry public wounds from a private vocation they did not choose, raised under scrutiny and often raised resentful of the church and the God it claims. This chapter names the PK wound and the church's hand in it.
chapters.body:
No one asks the children. That is the first thing to say and it should never stop being said. A man hears a call. A woman, sometimes, marries into it. But the children are born into a vocation already in progress, handed a public life before they can speak, raised in a glass house they did not build, and then judged for how they behave inside it. They never volunteered. They were conscripted at birth, and the church has spent generations pretending they enlisted.

The phenomenon has a name in church circles, half affectionate and half cruel: PK, pastor's kid. The affection hides the cruelty. The cruelty is this — the pastor's child grows up under a scrutiny applied to no other child in the congregation, held to a standard the deacons' children are not held to, watched for any sign of sin that might embarrass the office, and loved, when he is loved, partly as a reflection of his father rather than as a boy in his own right. He learns young that his misbehavior is not merely his own; it is a referendum on his father's fitness to lead. He learns that the family's standing in the only community they have depends, in some measure, on his good conduct. That is an unbearable weight to put on a ten-year-old, and the church puts it there without a flicker of awareness that it is doing anything at all.

I have five sons. I will guard their privacy as fiercely in this chapter as I have in every other, which means I will tell you nothing of them specifically and everything of the pattern I have watched in ministry families across the years. The pattern is a child who comes to associate the church with loss — the loss of his father to meetings, the loss of his privacy to the congregation's gaze, the loss of an ordinary anonymous childhood — and who, around adolescence, begins to direct his anger somewhere. Sometimes at the father. Sometimes at the church. Often, most tragically, at God, because God is the rival who took his dad, and no one ever gave him permission to be angry at God, so the anger goes underground and comes back later as departure.

We call these young people prodigals when they leave, and we cite the parable as though it consoles us, and we forget that in the parable the father runs (Luke 15:20). He does not stand on the porch cataloguing the son's failures. He runs, undignified, robe gathered up, an old man sprinting toward a boy who wasted everything. The church loves to quote that parable about other people's children. It rarely asks whether it helped manufacture the prodigals in the parsonage by treating them as extensions of an office instead of as souls.

Hear me carefully, because there is a self-implication here I cannot escape. I was raised without a father. I know, from the inside of the wound, what the absence of a father does to a boy — how it shapes everything afterward, how a man spends decades building back what was taken. And knowing that, I entered a vocation famous for taking fathers away from their sons in plain sight, with the congregation's blessing, in the name of God. The danger I am most qualified to warn against is the one I am most capable of committing. A man who lost his father can become so committed to the work of fathering everyone else's children in the faith that he becomes, to his own sons, the very absence he swore to end. I write this chapter against myself before I write it against you.

But the church has its own account to settle, and it is large. You watch these children. Stop it. You hold them to standards their peers escape. Stop it. You speak about them in the foyer in ways you would never speak about your own — the daughter who dresses like the world, the son who is wild, as if their souls were a quality-control problem in your purchased product. You have forgotten that these are children. The office is the father's. The child carries none of it and should be made to carry none of it. He is a boy who likes whatever boys his age like and who would, if you let him, simply be a member of the church rather than a symbol of its leadership. You will not let him. You made him a symbol the day he was born, and symbols are not allowed to be children, and the resentment that grows in a child forbidden to be a child is a resentment the church has earned.

Jesus was unambiguous about children and about the weight of harming them. *Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea* (Matthew 18:6). We apply that verse to abusers and predators, rightly. We never apply it to the slow, respectable causing-to-stumble that a congregation works on its pastor's children through years of scrutiny and quiet cruelty until the child concludes that the church is a place of judgment and the God of the church a thief of fathers. There is more than one way to make a little one stumble. Some of them happen at potlucks.

There is a hard word for the pastor and it is the hardest in the book. Your children will remember whether you came home. Not the sermons. Not the size of the church. They will remember whether your face lit up when you saw them or whether you looked, even for a second, like they were one more demand on a man already spent. They will remember whether the faith you preached was the faith they saw in the kitchen, or whether the public man and the private man were two men, because children can smell that hypocrisy at fifty yards and it will inoculate them against the gospel for life. You will preach to hundreds about the love of the Father. The test is whether five boys believed in fatherly love because they had felt it from you.

You cannot raise a child to despise the church and then mourn that he left it. The despising is taught, by a thousand small lessons, in the glass house, and both the pastor and the congregation hold the chalk. The remedy is not complicated, only costly. Let them be children. Defend their ordinariness. Love them for nothing — for no reflected credit, no good behavior, no usefulness to the man up front. Love them the way the Father loves, which is to say before they have done anything, and after they have done everything wrong, and all the way down the road while they are still a long way off. Run toward them. The church should be teaching the pastor to run toward his children, not handing him one more reason to stay late.
chapters.verdict: You cannot raise a child to despise the church and then mourn that he left it.
reflect: Do you hold the pastor's children to a standard you would never impose on your own?
When you speak about the pastor's family, would you say it to the children's faces?
Have you ever loved a pastor's child as a child, with no thought of how he reflects on the man up front?

chapters.title: The Wages of the Word
chapters.summary: The church underpays the man it claims to honor, hiding neglect behind a theology of sacrifice that costs the pastor's family their security. This chapter calls financial neglect what it is.
chapters.body:
There is a verse the church loves to quote at the pastor and hates to obey for him. *Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching* (1 Timothy 5:17). Double honor. And the very next verse removes any doubt that money is meant: *For the Scripture says, You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain, and, The laborer deserves his wages* (1 Timothy 5:18). Paul reaches for two texts about pay. He is not being delicate. He is saying the man who feeds you should be able to feed his own family, and a church that lets him go hungry has muzzled the ox.

We have built an entire spiritual vocabulary to avoid that verse. We praise the pastor's sacrifice, by which we mean his poverty. We commend his humility, by which we mean his silence about the salary. We tell him, sometimes from the pulpit he is not standing in that week, that the ministry is its own reward, that money is worldly, that a true man of God does not preach for filthy lucre — and every one of those true statements becomes, in the budget meeting, a tool for paying him less. The theology of sacrifice is real. The church has weaponized it. We use the pastor's genuine willingness to suffer for the gospel as cover for our own unwillingness to part with the money that would keep his children's teeth healthy.

I want to be exact about the mechanism, because it hides so well. No church board says, let us underpay the pastor. They say, we must be good stewards. They say, the budget is tight this year. They say, we don't want the pastor to be in it for the money, as if a living wage were a temptation to greed. And meanwhile the building gets its new roof, the sound system gets its upgrade, the parking lot gets repaved, and the man who is the actual ministry of the church goes home to a wife doing the math at the kitchen table after the kids are asleep, deciding which bill waits another month. The church spends freely on what it can see and tightly on the man it has decided should not need much. What a church funds is a confession. Read the budget and you will know the god.

The cruelty compounds across a career. The young pastor is paid little because he is young. The mid-career pastor is paid little because the church got used to paying him little. And the old pastor arrives at the end of a life of ministry with no retirement, no savings, a parsonage he must vacate, and a denomination or congregation that suddenly discovers it has no plan for him, because it never imagined he would age, because it never treated him as a man with a body that wears out and a future that requires provision. We consume his strong years and discard his weak ones. We do to the pastor at seventy what we deny we did to him at thirty.

Paul refused to let the Galatians hide behind false humility on this point. *Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches* (Galatians 6:6). Share. The teaching is not free. It cost the teacher years of study, a life of availability, the surrender of every other career he might have had. The congregation that receives the word for free and gives back as little as it can has not been generous and frugal. It has been a thief of the laborer's wages, and it has wrapped the theft in the language of stewardship, and God is not deceived by accounting.

There is a self-implication I owe here, and it is the pastor's complicity again. Brother, our false humility funds this. We perform contentment we do not feel because we are afraid that to ask for fair pay is to look unspiritual, and we would rather our families bleak quietly than risk the congregation thinking us mercenary. So we say nothing. We let the board feel generous at a number we know is thin. We absorb the shortfall in our own marriages, in the vacations we don't take, in the savings we never build, and we call our silence faith when it is partly cowardice and partly a pride that cannot bear to be seen needing. I have made that choice. It did not protect my family. It protected my image, and my image was not worth what it cost them.

But the church holds the budget, and so the church holds the larger guilt. You have the power here, not the pastor. You set the number. You decide whether the man who buries your dead can bury his own without going into debt. You decide whether his children go to the dentist. You decide whether his wife works a second job not from calling but from necessity while still being expected to fulfill the unpaid role we examined two chapters ago. The pastor cannot vote himself a raise without looking like exactly the kind of man you have trained him to fear being seen as. The decency has to come from you, unprompted, because you went looking for what he needed instead of waiting for him to humiliate himself by asking.

There is a tell, and you should learn it. When a church starts talking about the pastor's humility in the context of his salary, money is about to be saved at his family's expense. Watch for it. The appeal to his virtue is the anesthetic applied before the cut. A church genuinely concerned with the pastor's humility would pay him generously and then privately, lovingly, watch that the generosity did not corrupt him. Instead we use the word humility to mean keep him poor, and we feel righteous doing it, which is the deepest poison of all — a sin that congratulates itself.

A church that can afford its building and cannot afford its pastor has told you what it worships. It worships the building. It worships the program, the visible thing, the asset on the books. It does not worship the God who said the laborer deserves his wages, because if it did, the laborer would have his wages, and his children would be secure, and his wife would not be doing arithmetic in the dark. The budget is the most honest document the church produces. It does not know how to lie. Read it, and then go home and ask your God whether the ox you have been treading on the grain has been allowed to eat.
chapters.verdict: A church that can afford its building and cannot afford its pastor has told you what it worships.
reflect: Do you know whether your pastor can pay his bills, or have you been careful not to know?
Would your church's budget survive being read aloud as a statement of its true priorities?
When did concern for the pastor's "humility" last save the church money?

chapters.title: The Pedestal Is a Cage
chapters.summary: The church's habit of idealizing the pastor isolates him from honesty, forbids him weakness, and falls into contempt the moment he proves human. This chapter dismantles the pedestal as a form of cruelty disguised as honor.
chapters.body:
The pedestal looks like honor. It is a cage, and the bars are made of expectation, and the man inside it cannot move without being seen to fall.

We put the pastor up there for reasons we do not examine. We tell ourselves it is respect for the office, reverence for the calling, the proper dignity owed a man who handles holy things. Some of that is real. But underneath the honorable reasons lives a dishonorable one, and it is this: a pastor on a pedestal is a pastor we do not have to know. Distance is the point. If he is exceptional, super-spiritual, a man of a different order, then we are excused from the labor of friendship, excused from carrying him, excused from the discomfort of his ordinary humanity. We make him a saint so we can leave him alone. The pedestal is a way of admiring a man instead of loving him, and admiration costs nothing.

It also costs him everything. A man on a pedestal cannot be honest, because honesty would topple the statue, and the congregation that built the statue would experience its fall as betrayal. So he learns to manage the height. He stops admitting doubt, because the saint does not doubt. He stops admitting fear, because the man of faith is not afraid. He stops admitting the marriage is hard, the depression is real, the prayer life has gone dry, the call feels like a weight he cannot carry — because every one of those admissions would crack the plaster, and he has learned that the congregation does not want the man, it wants the statue. So he gives them the statue and quietly, alone, the man behind it starves.

This is not what God's people are supposed to think about their leaders. Scripture is relentlessly honest about its heroes, and the honesty is mercy. David, the man after God's own heart, is shown to us as an adulterer and an accessory to murder (2 Samuel 11). Elijah, fresh off the greatest public victory of his prophetic life, is shown collapsed under a tree begging God to let him die (1 Kings 19:4). Peter, the rock, is shown denying with curses that he ever knew the Lord (Matthew 26:74). The Bible does not pedestal its leaders. It tells the truth about them, and the truth is that they were men, gloriously used and deeply flawed, and the telling of their flaws is precisely what makes their God look great rather than making them look great. A church that needs its pastor to be flawless has a smaller view of grace than the Bible has.

There is a cruelty built into the pedestal that does not show until later, and it is the cruelty of the fall. Because here is what happens to the idealized man: the moment he proves human — the moment he loses his temper, makes a bad call, says the wrong thing, reveals a struggle — the very congregation that idealized him turns. The admiration curdles into contempt with astonishing speed, because the people were never in relationship with the man; they were in relationship with the image, and when the man cracks the image they feel deceived, though he deceived no one. He never claimed to be the statue. They built it. And now they punish him for not being the thing they made.

I have watched it happen to good men. A pastor serves faithfully for fifteen years, and the congregation speaks of him in tones near worship, and then one season he is tired and short-tempered and human, or he takes one unpopular stand, and within months the same people who idolized him are circulating their disappointment, and the fall is steeper precisely because the pedestal was so high. The height that felt like honor becomes the distance of the drop. We did that. We built the platform that made the wound mortal. A man at ground level who stumbles skins his knee. A man on a pedestal who stumbles breaks his neck, and we hold the wood.

Bonhoeffer, who knew something about idealized communities, wrote in *Life Together* that the man who loves his dream of community more than the community itself becomes a destroyer of community, even when his intentions are honest and earnest and sacrificial. The pedestal is the church in love with its dream of a pastor more than with the pastor. We want the dream — the flawless shepherd, the answer to every question, the man whose family is perfect and whose faith never wavers — and our love for that dream makes us destroyers of the actual man, whom we cannot see past the figure we have imagined onto him. Bonhoeffer said the dream-lover acts as judge over the brethren and over God. The congregation on the pedestal-building project has made itself judge over its pastor, sentencing him in advance to be cast down the day he is finally, unforgivably, real.

What does it cost to take him off the pedestal? It costs you the comfort of distance. It means coming close enough to discover that he is a man — sinful, struggling, ordinary in most things, gifted in a few — and loving him there, at ground level, the way you would love a brother and not the way you would venerate a relic. It means letting him be wrong without it being a crisis of the institution. It means letting him grieve, doubt, and rest, and not reading those as failures of office. It means, in short, the harder and humbler thing: friendship instead of fandom, knowing instead of admiring, the costly nearness instead of the cheap height.

You did not lift him up to honor him. You lifted him up so you would not have to know him. That is the verdict, and it will offend, and I will let it. The honor that requires distance is not honor; it is abandonment with a good view. The man up there is cold and the air is thin and he cannot tell you, because telling you would end the only standing he has left. Take him down. Take him down gently, and stand next to him, and find out who he actually is. You may discover you never knew the man at all. You only ever knew the statue you built so that knowing the man would not be required of you.
chapters.verdict: You did not lift him up to honor him; you lifted him up so you would not have to know him.
reflect: Do you want your pastor to be holy, or only to appear so on your behalf?
What happens in your church the first time the pastor is publicly wrong?
Have you mistaken admiration for love, when love would have required you to come closer?

chapters.title: When the Shepherd Breaks
chapters.summary: Burnout is not a failure of the pastor's faith but the predictable result of an unsustainable arrangement, and the church responds to the breaking with judgment instead of care. This chapter looks at the moment of collapse without flinching.
chapters.body:
There is a moment, and most long-serving pastors can name it, when the machine that has been running on fumes finally seizes. It is rarely dramatic from the outside. He does not collapse in the pulpit. More often it is a Tuesday, and he cannot make himself get out of the car, or he reads a familiar passage and feels nothing, or he hears that another family is leaving and instead of grief he feels relief, and the relief frightens him more than the leaving. Something inside has gone quiet that used to make noise. He is not backslidden. He is not faithless. He is burned out, which is a different thing, and the church does not know the difference and will judge him as the first when he is suffering the second.

Let me say what burnout is, because the church keeps misdiagnosing it as a spiritual failure and prescribing more of the disease as the cure. Burnout is what happens to a system run beyond its capacity for too long with no recovery. It is a physical and emotional condition with spiritual consequences, not a spiritual condition with physical symptoms. The man has poured out and not been refilled, given and not received, carried and not been carried, for years, and the well that he thought was bottomless turns out to have been fed by a spring he never tended, and one day there is no more water and he is still expected to pour. He does not need to be rebuked for emptiness. He needs to be told it is alright to be empty, and then he needs the church to do the unthinkable thing — to give to him for a season instead of taking.

The data, kept general as honesty requires, points one direction. Studies of clergy across the decades describe a population under chronic strain — high demand, low control over their time, blurred boundaries between work and home and self, isolation, and a culture that treats exhaustion as devotion. A significant number of those who enter ministry leave it, and a sobering share of those who stay are running on something close to fumes. I will not pin a false decimal on it. The general truth is stark enough. We are using men up. The pastorate, as the modern church has structured it, is a role that breaks a meaningful number of the men who attempt it, and we respond to the breaking as though the man were defective rather than the arrangement.

Even Elijah breaks, and the way God handles it should silence every church that has ever shamed a burned-out pastor. After Carmel, after fire from heaven, after the greatest day of his ministry, Elijah runs into the wilderness and sits under a broom tree and asks to die: *It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life* (1 Kings 19:4). The man who called down fire wants to be dead. And what does God do? He does not rebuke him. He does not question his call. He sends an angel, and the angel does not preach. The angel cooks. *Arise and eat* (1 Kings 19:5). Twice. *The journey is too great for you* (1 Kings 19:7). God's response to his exhausted prophet is food, sleep, food again, and only much later, gently, a quiet voice and a renewed commission. Bread before correction. Rest before purpose. The church does it backwards. We bring the burned-out pastor correction and purpose and withhold the bread and the rest, and then we wonder why he does not recover.

Jesus knew the body has limits and honored them in his disciples. When the apostles came back from ministry overflowing with reports, he did not schedule a debrief and send them out again. *Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while* (Mark 6:31). The text gives the reason with painful relevance: *for many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat*. That is a description of every overworked pastor in the country — so many coming and going that there is no leisure even to eat. And the Lord's instruction was not push through. It was come away and rest. If the church will not give its pastor what Jesus gave his apostles, it should stop claiming to follow him on the matter.

Here is where the church's guilt sharpens to a point. When the shepherd breaks, you have a choice, and most churches choose wrong. You can ask what broke him — what in the arrangement, the isolation, the workload, the underpayment, the loneliness ground a faithful man to dust — and you can repent of your part and help him heal. Or you can decide that he is the problem, that he lacked the faith or the fortitude or the discipline, and you can quietly move him along and find a fresh man to break. The second is easier. It requires no self-examination. It preserves the arrangement. And it is what most churches do, which is why the supply of broken pastors never runs out and the lesson is never learned. We replace the man and keep the machine, and the machine is the thing that needs to die.

There is the matter of help, and most churches have made help impossible. Where does a pastor go when he is drowning? If he tells the elders, he risks his job. If he sees a counselor, he fears the congregation finding out. If he confesses to a friend in ministry, he fears it traveling. The structure that isolates him also seals every exit, so that the only way out he can see is the catastrophic one — resignation, scandal, collapse. The church must build a door he can walk through without losing everything: confidential care, a sabbatical that is not a euphemism for being eased out, real provision for a man to step back and heal and return. A church that has no such door has decided, in advance, that its broken pastors will be discarded rather than restored, and that decision is a sin against the body of Christ.

A pastor does not burn out from too much God. He burns out from too much church and not enough. Too many meetings, too many demands, too many secrets, too much performance, too much taking — and not enough of the actual presence of God that the church crowds out by keeping him too busy to seek it. The cruelest irony of the burned-out pastor is that the institution built to bring people to God starved its own leader of God by working him to death in God's name. The remedy is not to try harder. It is to build a church a man can serve for thirty years with his soul intact, and to treat the breaking of a shepherd not as a verdict on his weakness but as an indictment of the load. The load is too great. It always was. We just kept finding men willing to be crushed by it, and calling their crushing faithfulness.
chapters.verdict: A pastor does not burn out from too much God; he burns out from too much church and not enough.
reflect: When a leader in your church broke down, did the church ask what broke him, or only judge that he broke?
Do you have any way for a struggling pastor to get help that does not cost him his job?
Have you built a church a man can serve for thirty years, or one that uses men up and replaces them?

chapters.title: The Ministry of Being Carried
chapters.summary: The pastor must learn the discipline of receiving care, and the church must learn to give it, because a body where help flows only one direction is not a body at all. This chapter addresses the mutual repentance required of both.
chapters.body:
There is a sin pastors rarely confess because it disguises itself as virtue, and it is this: the refusal to be carried. The man who has built his identity on being the one who helps cannot bear to be helped, and he calls the inability strength, and it is weakness of the most dangerous kind, because it cuts him off from the very grace he preaches. I know this sin from the inside. It is mine. The hardest sentence I have ever had to say is help me, and I have a vocation that lets me avoid saying it forever, and the avoidance was killing me before I understood it as sin.

The pastor who cannot receive does not actually believe the gospel he proclaims. Think about it honestly. The gospel is the announcement that we are helpless and must be carried — that we cannot save ourselves, cannot earn it, cannot pay, and must receive everything as gift from a God who carries what we could never lift. A pastor who can preach that on Sunday and cannot live it on Monday, who can tell the congregation to cast their cares on Christ and cannot cast a single care on another human being, has revealed that the gospel is a thing he sells rather than a thing he has bought. The inability to receive care is, at bottom, a refusal of grace. It is works-righteousness wearing a clerical collar. I must be the strong one, I must not need, I must carry and never be carried — that is not faith. That is the oldest lie, that we can be as God, self-sufficient, needing no one.

Scripture forbids it directly. *Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ* (Galatians 6:2). One another. The command is mutual or it is meaningless. A pastor who bears every burden and lets no one bear his is not fulfilling the law of Christ; he is half-obeying it and calling the disobedience humility. The same Paul who said share with the one who teaches also wrote, *Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it* (1 Corinthians 12:27), and a body where one organ only gives and never receives is not healthy — it is a tumor of usefulness, a part that has forgotten it is a part. The pastor is a member of the body, not the body's external benefactor. He is supposed to need the others. His need is not a failure of his office. It is the proof that he belongs to the body and not above it.

So there is a discipline the pastor must learn, and it is harder than any sermon prep. He must learn to say I am not okay to someone safe. He must learn to let a meal be brought without immediately reciprocating. He must learn to sit in a circle of men and be the one who is prayed for rather than always the one who prays. He must accept the sabbath, the help, the gift, the carrying — and accept it without the frantic need to earn it back, because earning it back would be the works-righteousness reasserting itself. Eugene Peterson spent his ministry insisting that the pastor's first work is to be unbusy enough to pay attention to God, and you cannot pay attention to God while frantically proving you need nothing from anyone. The unbusy, receiving, carried pastor is closer to the gospel than the heroic, self-sufficient one the church prefers.

And the church has its half of this to repent of, which is the simple, staggering fact that most congregations have never once carried their pastor with nothing asked in return. Examine your church's history. Every act of care toward the pastor, was it not bundled with an expectation? The meal that came with a request. The kind word that preceded the criticism. The Pastor Appreciation Month that costs a card and a gift basket and changes nothing about the workload on the first of November. When did your church ever simply give to the man — cover his pulpit so he could rest with no agenda, send him and his wife away with no strings, sit with him in a hard season asking nothing, provide for him generously expecting no increased output? If you cannot find such a moment, then the relationship has been one-directional from the start, and you have been a congregation that takes from a man who only gives, and you have called the arrangement a church when it was closer to a transaction.

The body image in 1 Corinthians 12 is not decorative. Paul is making a structural argument. *The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you* (1 Corinthians 12:21), and crucially, the parts that seem weaker are indispensable, and the parts we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor. Apply it. The pastor has been treated as the part that needs nothing, the self-sufficient organ, and that is a denial of the body's basic nature. In a real body, every part needs every other. The hand washes the eye. The whole body protects the wound. When one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26). A church where the pastor suffers and the body does not even notice has failed at being a body. It has become an audience with an employee.

What does mutual carrying actually look like? It is unglamorous. It is a few people who decide, without fanfare, that they will know the pastor as a man and watch over his soul the way he watches over theirs. It is elders who ask about his marriage and mean it, who guard his rest as fiercely as he guards the doctrine, who would notice if he were drowning and act before he asked. It is a congregation that has internalized that their pastor is a sheep too, with a shepherd's burden but a sheep's need, and that the same care he extends must flow back to him or the body is diseased. It is, finally, repentance on both sides — the pastor repenting of the pride that will not receive, the church repenting of the consumption that will not give.

The shepherd who cannot be a sheep does not believe his own gospel. And the church that will only be carried and never carries has not understood what a body is. Both must change, and the change is not a program but a turning — the pastor turning to receive, the people turning to give, until the help in the church runs in both directions for the first time and the body becomes, at last, a body. The law of Christ is fulfilled in burdens borne mutually. Anything less is one man carrying a building and calling the weight his calling, while the building watches him stagger and praises his strength.
chapters.verdict: The shepherd who cannot be a sheep does not believe his own gospel.
reflect: Pastor — can you receive care, or only give it, and what does your inability reveal?
Church — have you ever simply carried your pastor with nothing asked in return?
What would it look like for the help in your church to flow in both directions for once?

chapters.title: A Brotherhood for the Lonely
chapters.summary: The isolation that breaks pastors will not be solved inside a single congregation; it requires the wider body — pastors caring for pastors across the lines that usually divide them. This chapter makes the case for brotherhood as necessity, not luxury.
chapters.body:
Some wounds cannot be healed inside the room where they were made. The pastor's isolation is one of them. A congregation can do much — it can take him off the pedestal, pay him fairly, protect his family, give him rest — but there is a specific loneliness it cannot cure, because the cure requires someone who stands where he stands, and no one in the congregation does. He needs brothers. He needs other pastors. And the modern church has arranged itself so that pastors are the least likely men in the world to have them.

Consider the arrangement honestly. The pastors of a given city are, structurally, competitors. They draw from the same pool of people. When a family leaves one church for another, one pastor's loss is another's gain, and both men know it, and that knowledge poisons the ground where friendship would grow. Add the busyness — every pastor stretched too thin to maintain relationships outside his own walls. Add the suspicion — different denominations, different convictions, the old habit of treating the man down the street as a rival theological tribe rather than a brother in the same trench. Add the fear of exposure — to befriend another pastor is to risk being known, and being known is the thing the isolated man has learned to fear most. The result is a profession full of men doing the same impossible job within miles of each other, every one of them lonely, every one of them assuming his loneliness is unique.

I founded the Pastors Connection Network out of that exact loneliness, and I have said so plainly already because I will not pretend the network is a strategy I devised from a position of strength. It is a confession. I was a pastor with no pastor, a shepherd with no shepherd, and I went looking for brothers and found that the looking itself was the rarest act, because most men had given up assuming brotherhood was available to them. What I learned in the building of it is the thing I most want the church to hear: the isolation is not the pastor's preference. It is the structure's product. Remove the barriers and the men come gladly, because the hunger was there all along, hidden under the performance of self-sufficiency.

Scripture never sends its leaders out alone. Look at the pattern and it is unbroken. Jesus sent the seventy-two not one by one but *two by two* (Luke 10:1). Paul does not work alone; he travels with Barnabas, then with Silas, then with Timothy and Titus and a company of named coworkers, and when he is in prison and most alone he writes asking for Mark and for his friends, because even the apostle could not do it solo (2 Timothy 4:11). When Paul and Barnabas split, the split is painful precisely because the partnership mattered (Acts 15:39). The New Testament knows nothing of the lone-ranger minister we have manufactured. Ministry in the Bible is a company of men, and the isolated pastor is not a biblical figure. He is a modern casualty.

Ecclesiastes names the stakes with cold clarity. *Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up* (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10). Woe to him who is alone when he falls. Read it as a description of the solitary pastor and it stops being poetry and becomes prophecy. He will fall — every man does, into discouragement, into temptation, into despair — and the only question is whether there is another to lift him up, and we have built a system in which the answer, for most pastors, is no. Then a man falls, alone, in a moral failure or a breakdown or a quiet exit, and we are shocked, and the shock is itself the evidence of our negligence, because Ecclesiastes told us three thousand years ago that the man alone has no one to lift him and will therefore stay down.

There is a reason the brotherhood must cross the lines that usually divide us. The fellowship a pastor needs cannot come only from the men inside his own narrow tribe, partly because there may be none nearby, and partly because the relationships within a denomination carry their own politics — the man who could lift you is also the man on the committee that evaluates you. The brotherhood that heals is often the one built across the lines, with men who share the burden of the office even when they differ on second-order convictions, men who want nothing from you because there is nothing structural to want. I am Reformed in my convictions and I hold them without apology, and I have also learned that a brother who shares the weight of shepherding souls can be a true brother across a good deal of difference, because the loneliness of the office is ecumenical, and so the comfort must be too.

The church has a duty here it has never imagined as a duty. You must guard your pastor's brotherhood. You must see his time with other pastors not as time stolen from you but as the maintenance that keeps the man alive for you. Pay for the retreat. Cover the pulpit. Send him to the gathering of brothers and tell him to go without guilt. And then — this is the hard part — do not resent it when he comes back having given his deepest honesty to men who are not you, because his deepest honesty was never safe to give you, and the brotherhood is the place he can be the broken human being he cannot be in your sight. Begrudging him that is begrudging him oxygen.

A pastor with no brothers is a soldier with no army, and we have sent thousands out alone. We have commissioned them, prayed over them, sent them to the front, and then severed them from every other soldier and wondered at the casualty rate. The fix is not more conferences on technique. It is brotherhood — durable, confidential, mutual, the kind of company God has always given his leaders and the modern church has systematically denied them. Build it. Guard it. Pay for it. And if your pastor has even one brother who knows him fully and wants nothing from him, thank God, because that one brother may be the reason he is still standing — and if he has none, you have your answer about why the next breaking is only a matter of time.
chapters.verdict: A pastor with no brothers is a soldier with no army, and we have sent thousands out alone.
reflect: Does your pastor have even one peer who knows him fully and wants nothing from him?
Has your church ever paid for your pastor to invest in friendship with other pastors, or only in skills?
Are you guarding your pastor's brotherhood, or quietly resenting the time it takes?

chapters.title: From Consuming to Caring
chapters.summary: The book's call lands on the church as concrete repentance and a different way of holding the pastor — not better feelings but changed behavior toward the man and his family. This final chapter names the turn and leaves the weight.
chapters.body:
A book like this is easy to read and easy to set down, and the setting-down is the danger, because the words can produce a feeling that is mistaken for repentance and changes nothing. So let this last chapter refuse the comfortable closing. The turn from consuming to caring is not a feeling. It is a set of changed behaviors, costly and specific, and if your church does not do anything differently next month, then you have not been moved; you have only been entertained by your own conviction.

Begin with the order God set and the church reversed. The pastor's family is the first flock. Defend it. That means your church builds a schedule that assumes the pastor has a marriage and children, not one that treats his family as the slack to be taken up whenever the church wants more. It means you protect his evenings, his sabbath, his vacation, his anniversary, and you do not punish him in his heart or his review for the time he keeps at home. It means you treat his wife as a person with her own calling and her own limits, free to serve where she is gifted and free to decline where she is not, shielded from the gossip that treats her as public property. It means you let his children be children — ordinary, unwatched, loved for nothing, defended from the scrutiny you would never accept for your own. The first flock is not yours to consume. Guard it as if you will answer for it, because you will.

Then pay him. Not what you can get away with — what the labor is worth. Read your budget as the confession it is, and ask whether the man who is the actual ministry of your church can pay his bills, secure his old age, and send his children to the dentist without his wife doing arithmetic in the dark. Stop using the language of his humility to fund your frugality. The laborer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18), and a church that funds its building and starves its pastor has confessed its god in a ledger. Change the ledger. Repentance you can read in a spreadsheet is the only kind that has weight.

Then take him off the pedestal and come close. Stop admiring him at a distance that excuses you from knowing him. Let him be a man — wrong sometimes, tired sometimes, afraid sometimes — and do not turn on him the moment he proves human, because the turning was always the cruelty hidden inside the height. Build him a door he can walk through when he is drowning: confidential care that does not cost him his job, a sabbatical that is not a quiet firing, real provision for him to heal and return. And guard his brotherhood — pay for it, cover the pulpit, send him to the men who share the weight, and do not resent the honesty he gives them that he could never safely give you. Carry him. Carry him with nothing asked in return, because a body where help runs one direction is not a body, and the man has been the hand that washes every eye and has never once had his own wound washed.

Hear the Scripture that should govern every leadership meeting and never does. *Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you* (Hebrews 13:17). The church loves the first half — obey your leaders — and ignores the second, which is the hinge. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning. The text assumes the congregation has power over whether the watching is joyful or grievous. You can make it joy. You can make it groaning. And the warning is that the groaning is of no advantage to you — a pastor ground down to groaning cannot give you what a pastor sustained in joy can. Your care for him is not charity you extend from surplus. It is the condition of receiving the ministry you say you want.

And do not miss what the writer of Hebrews asks of the people directly: *Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith* (Hebrews 13:7). Remember them. Consider how their life turned out. The church is meant to watch the whole arc of a pastor's life and learn from how it ended — and what an indictment, then, that we so often arrange for it to end in exhaustion, in collapse, in a discarded man with no provision and a wounded family. We are writing the outcome of his way of life with our treatment of him, and one day the younger believers will consider that outcome, and what they see will preach louder than anything he said from the pulpit.

There is a self-implication I owe at the end, and it is the whole reason I could write this book. I have been the consumed pastor and the consuming one. I have let my family pay for a ministry they did not choose. I have refused to be carried and called the refusal strength. I built a network for lonely pastors because I was the lonely pastor, and the founding was a confession before it was ever a strategy. I write none of this from a height. I write it from the floor, as a man who has made every error this book names and is still, by grace, standing — and standing largely because, late, I let myself be carried. Do not hear a finished man lecturing a failing church. Hear a brother who learned this at cost and would spare you some of the cost.

One day you will give an account for the shepherd you were given, and you will not be asked how he served you. You will be asked how you held him. Whether you spent him or carried him. Whether his family thrived in your midst or was slowly used up while you praised his devotion. Whether you took him off the pedestal and loved the man, or built the statue higher and walked away. The account is coming, and the question on it is already written, and it is not the question you have been answering on Sunday mornings. You have been keeping score of his ministry to you. God has been keeping a different book. Open it now, while there is still a man to carry and a family to defend and time, by grace, to change the outcome you are writing every week with your hands.

The shepherd is also a sheep. Go and find him on the hillside, alone in the open where you left him, and bring him home.
chapters.verdict: One day you will give an account for the shepherd you were given, and you will not be asked how he served you.
reflect: What is the one concrete thing your church could change this month that would lighten your pastor's actual load?
If your pastor's family read this book, would they recognize your church as a place that cared for them, or one that used them?
Whose account are you living toward — the church's verdict on your pastor, or God's verdict on you?
